chapter_theme: Marutham: the wife turns away the bard who pleads for her straying husband (21-23), then tells her friend of her anger, her faded beauty, the son his father passed by on the way to a new wedding, and the union she still finds sweet (24-30).

21.reading: The wife tells the bard that in pressing her to trust the word of the man of the wide town he is no different from those who hawk fine-eyed needles in the smiths' own street, taking any goods offered for them.
21.nuance: The smiths' street is where needles are made, so selling them there is the proverbial wasted errand: she knows the man's word better than any go-between can describe it. The bard is mocked, not answered.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife turns away the bard who pleads for the man of the town

comparisons.tenor: the bard urging the wife to trust her husband's word

22.reading: The wife asks the bard who roams as envoy for the man of the watered fields where bees hum at the blossoms what he has come into her house to do, out of his wits, and points him to the road to her 'younger sisters'' houses.
22.nuance: எங்கையர், 'our younger sisters', is the wife's barbed courtesy for the other women. The bee that moves among blossoms is only the town's scene here; read as the husband moving among women it would make one match, short of a hidden comparison.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife refuses the bard of the man of the watered fields

23.reading: The wife asks the bard whether the grace of the man of the wide, rich fields needs to be pleaded for, since the bond of those who know what ought to be known will itself show the way.
23.nuance: The argument turns the bard's office against itself: if the man felt the bond, no envoy would be needed; that an envoy comes proves the bond is missing.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard pleads for the husband and is turned away

ullurai.tenor: the husband who keeps to other women's houses for fear of his wife's anger

pairs.situation: he dreads the wife's sharp reproach
he hides among the other women

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the heron and fish of the pond of her own marutham town (porul 7.26)

24.reading: For the man of the town where the vaalai fish, afraid of the stab of the handsome little heron, hides among the blue lilies, our shoulders were once sandal paste to lean on; in this season they are hotter than caustic.
24.nuance: The fish fleeing the heron's beak into the lilies maps onto the husband who, dreading the wife's sharp words, hides in other women's houses; her shoulders, once his cooling sandal, now burn him.

thinai_evidence.note: the pond fish, heron and blue lily of the watered fields

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, once cool and welcome to him
her shoulders now, burning with anger

25.reading: Should the pain of longing for the desirable chest of the man of the fine-field town, where lotuses open like flame, come upon her, the wife says it is eased by the earnest prattle of her little son with the curling tuft.
25.nuance: The sentence leaves its verb unsaid, so the boy's chatter may either console her without the man or soften her toward him; either way the child, not the bard, is the go-between who works.

thinai_evidence.note: the lotus fields and the straying husband's chest

comparisons.tenor: the lotus opening red as flame

26.reading: The wife tells her bangled friend to see what happened when, as the drums of the man's new wedding, already the town's great joke, were sounding, this little one ran after him mounting his decorated chariot, reached him and came to grief.
26.nuance: இவன், 'this one', is most naturally the son (as in 28), turned away at the chariot by a father bound for another bride; it could also be the bard, who went to the wedding and was rebuffed.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the fields takes another bride and his wife is hurt

27.reading: The wife asks whether she is still the kind the man of the cool fields would quarrel with, now that her five-part hair has thinned like fine grains and her skin has turned pale like the white marul fibre, changed in colour.
27.nuance: To sulk at someone is to still want her; she says she has faded past even being worth his anger, so his absence is not oodal but neglect.

thinai_evidence.note: the sulk of the man of the cool fields

28.reading: The wife tells her sword-eyed friend that her heart has hardened against the man of the town of loud-sounding waters, because, while her son stood there longing, he did not tell the chariot to stop, saw him and drove on without a glance.
28.nuance: The charge is precise: he saw (கண்டு) and did not look (நோக்கான்). The son's mute yearning (ஏக்கற்று) is the appeal that fails, and her hardening follows from his hardness to the child, not to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's anger at the man of the watered town

29.reading: The wife tells her friend that she would say 'I will not embrace his wide chest', but does the man of the loud waters care at all that she refuses? She will go on doing his bidding.
29.nuance: The refusal is withdrawn not from desire but because it has no audience: oodal is a weapon only against someone who notices it.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife weighs refusing the husband's embrace

30.reading: The wife tells her bright-jewelled friend that as the south wind is sweet to the body when it blows even in the cold season, so union with the man's fragrant body is sweet to her even while she sulks.
30.nuance: The comparison is pointed: the south wind belongs to a warm season, so its sweetness out of season is like a union that pleases against her own quarrel.

thinai_evidence.note: sulking and union with the man of the town

comparisons.vehicle: குளிரும் பருவத்தே யாயினும் தென்றல் வளியெறியின் மெய்யிற்(கு) இனிதாம்
comparisons.tenor: union with the man while she sulks

links.note: Both wives turn away the bard over the husband's வாய்மொழி: Akananuru 146 pities the woman who will trust that deceiver's word as she once did; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 says the bard who asks her to trust it is hawking needles in the smiths' street.
links.teaches: Akananuru 146 shows the wife as a past victim of the man's word, and 21 shows why that history makes the bard's pleading absurd: she is the one market where his word cannot be sold.

links.note: Natrinai 200 has the friend warn the town's women against the bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 treats his pleading not as dangerous but as pointless.
links.teaches: The two refusals name two faults in the go-between, falsehood that endangers others and futility before the wife who already knows, so the refusal of the bard had both a public and a private argument.

links.note: In Akananuru 56 the wife tells the bard who blundered into her house 'இம்மனை அன்று; அஃது உம்மனை'; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 22 she tells him 'நெறிஅதுகாண் எங்கையர் இற்கு'.
links.teaches: The same retort appears as a told comic incident in Akananuru and as a direct taunt in the four-line venba, which shows that pointing the bard to the other house was a fixed refusal move the later poet could use bare, without the story.

links.note: Kural 785: shared feeling alone, without meeting or acquaintance, gives the claim of friendship. Ainthinai Aimpathu 23: the bond of those who know needs no bard to plead for the man's grace.
links.teaches: The wife turns the Kural's rule about friendship into an argument against intercession in marriage: if feeling alone makes the bond, then the presence of a go-between is itself proof that the feeling is gone.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 376 the man says his beloved is cool like Pothiyil sandal in summer and warm like a lotus heart in the cold; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 24 the wife says her shoulders were once sandal paste to him and are now hotter than caustic.
links.teaches: The lover's praise of a body that tempers every season is answered by the wife's claim that the same body's heat follows his conduct, not the weather, so the courtship image is shown to depend on fidelity.

links.note: In Kalittokai 81 the son's prattle is praised as 'நோய் நாம் தணிக்கும் மருந்து', the medicine that eases our illness; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 25 the pain of longing for the man's chest is met by the son's மழலைவாய் கட்டுரை.
links.teaches: Both make the child's prattle the cure for the wife's love-sickness in a marutham quarrel, and Kalittokai's longer scene shows what the venba compresses: the boy repeats words learned in the street, so his chatter can carry the father back into the house.

links.note: Kural 66: only those who have not heard their children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல்) call the flute and lute sweet. Ainthinai Aimpathu 25: the son's மழலைவாய் talk eases the pain of longing for the husband.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks prattle above music as a pleasure; the venba gives it a harder task, standing in for an absent husband's embrace, so the general praise of children is tested in the one place it might fail.

links.note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, dressed for a new wedding, stops his chariot when his son runs to him and gives the wedding up; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 26, as the drums of his new wedding sound, the little one who goes after his chariot comes to grief. On the reading of இவன் as the son, the appeal that succeeds in one fails in the other.
links.teaches: Akananuru 66 presents the son as the force that turns a husband back from another marriage, and 26 shows the same scene with the opposite outcome, so the son's claim emerges as a hope the wives hold rather than a rule the poems guarantee.

links.note: Akananuru 66: seeing the son run to him, the man cries 'நெடுந்தேர் தாங்குமதி, வலவ!' and climbs down. Ainthinai Aimpathu 28: the son stands yearning, the man sees him and drives the chariot on without a look.
links.teaches: Set side by side the two chariots mark the test of a straying husband as whether he stops for his child, and 28 makes the wife's hardening a verdict on his failing that test rather than on his other women.

links.note: Kural 1309: sulking, like water in the shade, is sweet only with those who love. Ainthinai Aimpathu 27: the faded wife asks whether she is still one the man would sulk at.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule that a quarrel belongs inside love lets the wife read the man's absence of pulavi as the absence of love, so the venba shows the rule used as evidence by someone on the losing side.

links.note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering when there is no lover who knows we suffer? Ainthinai Aimpathu 29: she would refuse his embrace, but he has no thought of her refusal, so she will serve him.
links.teaches: Both say a protest needs a lover who registers it, and the venba draws the practical end the couplet stops short of: with no such lover, the wife abandons oodal and goes back to service.

links.note: Kural 1330: sulking is love's pleasure, and its pleasure is to embrace after it. Ainthinai Aimpathu 30: even while sulking, union with the man's fragrant body is sweet, like the south wind in the cold season.
links.teaches: The Kural places the embrace after the sulk, while the wife finds it sweet during the sulk itself, so the venba collapses the Kural's sequence and shows desire overriding the quarrel instead of crowning it.

source_issues: 24 line 1: சறுகுருகின் reads as a misprint for சிறுகுருகின், the little heron.
27 line 2: நுண்ணுறல் is not a clear word; the hair thinned 'like fine ...' is uncertain, and the verse is marked uncertain. Line 1 தணவயல் is probably தண்வயல், cool fields.
21 line 1: கொண்டுழிப் பண்டம் விலையொரீஇ is hard to construe (taking goods in exchange instead of a price?); the needle-sellers' simile is clear but this clause is not.
All ten verses: the core record has no thurai, so speaker and addressee are inferred from the vocatives (பாண, பெய்வளைக் கையாய், வாட்கண்ணாய், புனையிழையாய், ஒளியிழாய்) and occasion words are null.
